prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks that reach a fractional uncertainty of 10^-18

statement.case_for: After reading the other ballots I keep optical lattice clocks first. Four of eight members put B001 first and two more put it second or third, which is the broadest base of support on the table, but I do not treat that as merit. The case is that this is a specific, identifiable invention: Katori's magic-wavelength lattice removes Doppler and recoil shifts while keeping many atoms, and Ye's group turned it into the 10^-18 systems that now drive tests of fundamental constants, dark-matter searches, relativistic geodesy and the roadmap to redefine the second. That matches how I understand the criterion, a discovery or invention rather than lifetime achievement, and the attribution is clean with two named people. Independent clocks at several national laboratories agree at this level, so the result does not depend on a single group's claim. Having read Kroll, Lindroth and Mehlig, none of them sees the 2005 comb prize as a real obstacle, and I agree: the comb is the readout tool, the lattice clock is a different invention.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that this is a measurement-and-instrument achievement in a field with several earlier prizes (1989, 2005, 2012), and a committee could judge that precision timekeeping has had its share. The credited names also omit other contributors (Lemonde, Takamoto, the NIST and JILA team members, the Yb groups), so a two-person split may look narrower than the community history. A further point is that the redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so a critic can say the practical payoff is still ahead.

responses.point: Pearce ranks the IceCube neutrino discovery first as an instrument-led opening of a new observational window, with Halzen as the single credited name.
responses.response: I accept the scientific weight of high-energy neutrino astronomy, and Pearce's own Borda score for B001 (rank 2) shows we overlap. My difficulty is attribution: a one-name prize for a cubic-kilometre collaboration invites exactly the objection Pearce raises in his own assessment, and the longlist gives us no way to widen it fairly. I would also note that source identification (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068) is still at moderate significance. I would keep B027 as a candidate for a later year rather than this one, unless the committee can find a defensible wider credit.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first, arguing it is a concrete prediction followed by a specific experiment with very broad impact, while admitting that credit for experimentalists beyond the lead group is unresolved.
responses.response: I agree this is the strongest condensed-matter case, I ranked it second, and the prediction-then-experiment structure is exactly what I look for. Where I differ is on timing and attribution. The pairing mechanism is still debated, as Danielsson and Eriksson both note, and Cao as first author, plus Dean, Young, Yacoby and others, are outside the credited trio. Giving the prize now would fix the allocation before the experimental history has settled. I would put B017 as the clear first alternative, and I would move it up if the committee thinks the field is already secure enough.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first as the architecture beneath essentially all superconducting quantum processors, and puts clocks third with the worry that a clock prize may overlap with 2005 and 2012.
responses.response: I take the architectural importance of circuit QED seriously, but it follows closely on the 2025 prize for macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits, which Kroll, Lindroth and Pearce all flag, and four credited names do not fit a three-person limit without leaving out Girvin or Blais. On the clock overlap, I do not think 2012 is a close precedent: Wineland and Haroche rewarded control of single quantum systems, while the lattice clock uses many neutral atoms and a different idea. I would ask Johansson whether the 2025 proximity is, for him, a reason to wait or only a presentational issue.

responses.point: Eriksson places tunnel magnetoresistance third as the natural second chapter after the 2007 GMR prize, and ranks twisted bilayer graphene and DMFT above it.
responses.response: We both ranked B015 third, and from my own interface work I find the MgO coherent-tunnelling story convincing. But I see the same attribution problem he describes: the 1995 room-temperature TMR and the 2004 MgO step were reached by overlapping groups (Yuasa and Djayaprawira are missing, and Butler and Mathon on the theory side), and the 2007 prize makes a second spintronics award harder to justify now. That is why B015 is not in my alternatives even though it is on my own ballot.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards a metrology prize in this area as sufficiently distinct from 2005 and 2012, and how much weight the pending redefinition of the second should carry.
How to weigh Katori's proposal against Ye's record-accuracy systems in the citation, and whether leaving out other clock contributors will be seen as unfair.
Whether B017 would be more convincing in a year or two once the pairing mechanism and the experimental credit are better settled.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile for B001, B017 or B010; my work is in transmission electron microscopy of interfaces and oxides, not clocks or moire materials. My only listed Chalmers connection is to Goran Johansson, and he did not rank any of my preferred candidates first. I did work on oxide interfaces (LaAlO3/SrTiO3), which is adjacent to B017 but involves no named candidate.
